title: Meeting Rooms II
corePattern: Sweep Line / Greedy Interval Partitioning - Maximum Concurrency Equals Minimum Resources
interviewTips: Clarify: is [1,2] and [2,3] overlapping? No - a meeting ending at time t frees the room for a meeting starting at t, so use < not <= when comparing start vs end.

Trade-off: Two-pointers on sorted starts/ends is O(n log n) time and O(n) space with best constants; Min-Heap is same complexity but more directly models room reuse and extends to assignment problems.
Edge-case tip: empty input returns 0, single interval returns 1, and brute-force counting pairwise overlaps overcounts - you must count concurrency at a point in time, not total overlapping pairs.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Counting at Start Times
approaches.intuition: The number of rooms needed equals the maximum number of meetings happening at the same instant. That maximum must occur at some meeting start time, so check every start time and count how many intervals cover it.
approaches.theory: For a fixed time t = intervals[i][0], a meeting j is active iff start_j <= t < end_j. Counting this for all i and taking the max yields the chromatic number of the interval graph. We evaluate n points against n intervals. Correctness follows because concurrency only increases at start events, so the peak is attained at a start.

timeComplexity.explanation: For each of n start times we scan all n intervals to count coverage.

edgeCases: Touching intervals [[1,2],[2,3]] => 1, must use < not <= for end check

approaches.name: Approach 2: Sorted Starts and Ends with Two Pointers
approaches.intuition: Sort all start times and all end times separately. Sweep chronologically: if the next start is before the earliest end, we need a new room; otherwise a room frees up and we reuse it.
approaches.theory: This is a sweep line / prefix-sum on events. Let starts and ends be sorted. Maintain used rooms. Invariant: ends[e] is the earliest ending among active meetings. If starts[s] < ends[e], no meeting has ended, so used++. Else, one meeting ended (used--) before starts[s], so we advance e to free it. Tracking max used gives answer. Sorting dominates cost.

timeComplexity.explanation: Sorting starts and ends dominates; linear two-pointer sweep after.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Two extra arrays of size n for starts and ends; sorting uses O(log n) stack.

approaches.name: Approach 3: Sort by Start + Min-Heap of End Times
approaches.intuition: Process meetings in start order. Keep a min-heap of end times of rooms currently in use. If the earliest-ending room is free (end <= current start), reuse it; otherwise allocate a new room. Heap size at the end is the answer.
approaches.theory: Greedy interval partitioning is optimal: sorting by start time and reusing any free room never harms optimality due to exchange argument - all busy rooms are symmetric except end time, so freeing the earliest-ending one is best. Min-heap gives O(log n) access to earliest end. Max heap size equals max concurrency, which is a lower bound and achieved by this construction.

timeComplexity.explanation: Sort by start O(n log n) plus n heap push/pop each O(log n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Heap holds at most n end times in worst case of all overlapping.

edgeCases: Chain [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]] => heap stays size 1 due to <= reuse
